updateCadence: Irregular; a few releases per year plus frequent development snapshots
summary: Lynx renders HTML as text in a terminal, with no JavaScript, images or CSS. It is ideal for SSH sessions, screen readers and low-end systems, but cannot use most modern web apps.
notFor: Anyone needing JavaScript, images or video

pros.title: Tiny and instant
pros.detail: Starts immediately and uses a few MB of RAM, even on very old hardware.

pros.title: No JavaScript attack surface
pros.detail: No JS, no CSS tracking tricks and no images means most tracking and ads never load.

pros.title: Accessibility friendly
pros.detail: Plain linear text output works well with braille displays and screen readers.

pros.title: Scriptable
pros.detail: Dump or fetch pages from the command line and customise keys through lynx.cfg.

pros.title: Everywhere
pros.detail: Packaged in nearly every Linux/BSD distro and Homebrew, with Windows builds by the maintainer.

cons.title: Most modern sites fail
cons.detail: No JavaScript means web apps, logins with JS flows and SPAs generally do not work.

cons.title: No images or media
cons.detail: Cannot display images or video itself, only hand them to external programs.

cons.title: Dated interface
cons.detail: Cursor-key link navigation and a config file are a steep learning curve for newcomers.

cons.title: Small security surface but old code
cons.detail: C codebase without modern sandboxing; TLS stack depends on OpenSSL/GnuTLS builds.

switching.note: No importers; bookmarks are a local file. Copy any URLs over manually.

spec.patchLag: Depends on distro and the system TLS library

pageLoad: Fast text fetch but renders only static HTML
installSize: Well under 2 MB binary in most distros
blocking: Ads and trackers mostly cannot run, no filter lists
securityHardening: No sandbox; C code, but no JS engine

featureNotes.adBlocker: Ads mostly absent as they need images/JS
featureNotes.keyboardShortcuts: Fully keyboard driven; keymap in lynx.cfg
